name: Flow

hero.title: Drag one node. Nothing else re-renders.
hero.lede: Node editors and diagrams on signals: nodes, edges, handles, pan and zoom, a minimap and seven layout algorithms, all built in. Each custom node mounts once and updates in place, and it beat React Flow 12 on all six operations we timed.

facts.value: 6 of 6 operations won<small>500 nodes, 499 edges, one run</small>

why.title: For workflow builders, pipelines and whiteboards.

items.title: Every node mounts once
items.text: A custom node gets accessors (`data()`, `selected()`, `dragging()`), not values. Dragging one node runs zero updates on the nodes and edges it does not touch, and the tests count them.

items.title: Layout in the box
items.text: `flow.layout()` runs layered, force, stress, tree, radial, box or rect-packing layouts on each node's measured size. No dagre, no elkjs; the engine loads on first use.

items.title: Connections without plumbing
items.text: Drop a handle on a handle and the edge exists. `isValidConnection` vetoes, `connectionRadius` snaps a near miss, and edges attach to the measured handle dots.

items.title: Editor chores, done
items.text: Undo and redo (50 steps by default), copy and paste, sub-flows, keyboard access, and `toJSON` / `fromJSON` that treats loaded data as untrusted.

difference.title: The state hooks go. The change handlers go.

before.label: React + React Flow 12
before.caption: Two state hooks, two change handlers and a memoised connect callback, all to let the user drag and connect.

after.label: with @pyreon/flow
after.caption: The instance owns its nodes and edges as signals. Dragging, selecting and connecting update it directly.

demo.title: Drag the nodes. Then auto-layout.
demo.text: Drag any node and the edges follow. "Auto-layout" runs the built-in layered engine on the measured node sizes. The counter shows how many times a node component has re-run since mount.
demo.referenceHtml: nodes re-mounted while dragging: 0
demo.spec: Build with a real @pyreon/flow instance (useFlow) and <Flow> with a custom node type for the seven workflow nodes (Webhook, Validate, Enrich, Score lead, CRM, Slack alert, Archive) and the six edges from the reference. "Auto-layout" calls flow.layout('layered', { direction: 'RIGHT' }) (animated, 300 ms by default); "Scramble" writes random positions through updateNodePosition. The counter is real: increment a module-level count inside the custom node component body and show it, so it reads 0 re-runs after mount however much the visitor drags, selects or lays out. Keep <Background variant="dots"> and add <Controls /> so pan and zoom are one click away.

items.name: `createFlow` and `useFlow`,
items.text: generic over your node data; `useFlow` disposes with the component.

items.name: Custom node and edge renderers
items.text: that read reactive accessors, so they mount once and patch in place.

items.name: Five path builders:
items.text: bezier, smoothstep, step, straight and waypoint routes, with markers, labels and per-edge `pathOptions`.

items.name: Seven layouts:
items.text: layered, force, stress, tree, radial, box and rect packing, animated and fed by measured node sizes.

items.name: Handles that measure themselves:
items.text: edges attach to each dot's rendered centre; handle-less nodes get floating endpoints.

items.name: Layout helpers:
items.text: sub-flows, `zIndex` with raise on select, snap to grid and to other nodes, auto-pan at the edge.

items.name: Culling for big graphs:
items.text: `onlyRenderVisibleElements` mounts only what is in view.

items.name: Theming:
items.text: 25 `--pyreon-flow-*` CSS variables and `colorMode` light, dark or system.

limits.title: Read node props as accessors
limits.text: Write `props.data().label`, not `props.data.label`. `data`, `selected` and `dragging` are accessors: call them where you render, and updates reach the node.

limits.title: Culling is opt-in
limits.text: Every node mounts by default. For a large graph, set `onlyRenderVisibleElements: true` and only what is in view stays in the DOM.

limits.title: Layout options depend on the algorithm
limits.text: `direction` applies to layered and tree; `layerSpacing` and `edgeRouting` to layered only. The others ignore them, with a dev warning.

limits.title: iOS and Android are experimental
limits.text: The native host draws SwiftUI and Compose views. Renderers styled with a `class` or `style`, `<ViewportPortal>` and `flowStyles` stay on the web; `<FlowWebView>` hosts the browser renderer when you need it.

benchmarks.rival: vs React Flow 12 · 500 nodes, 499 edges, real Chromium, M3 Max
benchmarks.h: Faster than React Flow 12 on all six operations.
benchmarks.p: Dragging a node is 7.25× faster because only that node and its edges update. Read the 210× pan-and-zoom row with care: on a viewport change Pyreon writes one CSS transform, while React Flow re-renders its node wrappers on every store write, so the gap measures that design difference more than raw speed. Neither arm synthesizes pointer events; both drive their public API and check the DOM on every iteration.

comingFrom.title: Drag, connect, minimap: no handlers to write.
comingFrom.note: The component names are the ones you know (`Background`, `Controls`, `MiniMap`, `Handle`, `NodeResizer`). The difference is ownership: the flow instance holds nodes and edges as signals, so a drop on a handle adds the edge and fires `onConnect` for you to observe, not to implement.

comingFrom.title: Custom nodes without memo.
comingFrom.note: A Pyreon node renderer runs once per node for the life of the graph. It reads `props.data()` and `props.selected()` where it renders them, so `updateNode` patches the text in place. No `memo`, and the `nodeTypes` map can live anywhere.

comingFrom.title: Auto-layout without a second library.
comingFrom.note: React Flow leaves layout to dagre, elkjs or d3-hierarchy, and you convert between their coordinates and yours. `flow.layout()` reads the measured node sizes itself, animates the move, and loads its engine on the first call.

recipes.title: A diagram that saves itself
recipes.text: Persist to `localStorage`, restore on load, and put undo and redo in a corner panel. `fromJSON` drops duplicate ids and dangling edges with a warning instead of crashing.

recipes.title: A workflow builder with rules
recipes.text: Refuse self-loops and connections into a trigger, default every edge to an animated smoothstep, and cull off-screen nodes for big workflows.

faq.q: Why is pan and zoom 210× faster?
faq.a: Because the two libraries do different work. On a viewport change Pyreon updates one CSS transform on the viewport element and creates no new elements (a test counts them). React Flow re-renders its node wrappers on every store write. Read it as a design difference (the record says the same of most of the drag gap), and look at select (5.39×) and unmount (3.87×) for a closer race.

faq.q: Is this React Flow ported to Pyreon?
faq.a: No. The vocabulary is close on purpose (`Handle`, `MiniMap`, `NodeResizer`, `isValidConnection`, `onlyRenderVisibleElements`), so the concepts carry over. Underneath, every node and edge has its own signals, and a node component never re-renders.

faq.q: How large a graph can it take?
faq.a: The benchmark graph is 500 nodes and 499 edges. A drag frame does a constant number of lookups whatever the graph size (a test compares 20 and 120 nodes). Past what fits on screen, turn on `onlyRenderVisibleElements`.

faq.q: Does it run on iOS and Android?
faq.a: Yes, experimentally. `createFlow` and `<Flow>` lower to a native SwiftUI or Compose host with the same instance API, all seven layouts, gestures and the minimap. It is a native view tree, not a WebView. Renderers that depend on CSS stay web-only, and the compiler names each one.

faq.q: What does the layout engine depend on?
faq.a: Nothing outside Pyreon. All seven algorithms are pure geometry in the package, split into their own chunk so the first `layout()` call loads them.
